clinicalPearls: Cone dysfunction dominates early, so patients describe reduced central acuity, colour-vision disturbance and photophobia before nyctalopia appears, in contrast to the reverse order seen in classic rod-cone retinitis pigmentosa
Genetically heterogeneous with autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive and X-linked inheritance; ABCA4 is a common recessive cause and CRX, GUCY2D and peripherin/RDS underlie dominant forms
Fundoscopy typically shows a bull's-eye or atrophic maculopathy with later peripheral pigmentary change and attenuated vessels as rod involvement supervenes

Full-field electroretinography demonstrates photopic (cone) responses depressed out of proportion to scotopic (rod) responses, the electrophysiological signature that separates it from rod-cone dystrophy
Optical coherence tomography shows loss of the outer retinal layers and ellipsoid zone at the fovea, and fundus autofluorescence often reveals a ring or bull's-eye of abnormal signal
Progressive by definition, distinguishing it from the stationary cone dysfunction syndromes, and central vision is affected relatively early
Management is supportive with refraction, tinted glasses or filters for glare, low-vision aids, genetic counselling and enrolment in registries or gene-therapy trials where relevant
reference.pathophysiology: Cone-rod dystrophy is a group of inherited retinal degenerations in which photoreceptor loss begins predominantly in the cones and later extends to the rods. Mutations in genes governing the phototransduction cascade, the visual cycle (for example ABCA4) or photoreceptor development and structure (for example CRX, GUCY2D, peripherin/RDS) impair cone metabolism and survival, causing early central and colour-vision failure. As the disease advances, rod photoreceptors also degenerate, producing peripheral field loss and night blindness, so the final picture can resemble widespread retinal dystrophy but with a cone-first temporal sequence.
additionalDifferentials: Rod-cone dystrophy (retinitis pigmentosa) with a rod-first pattern
Isolated cone dystrophy without rod involvement
Hydroxychloroquine or other toxic bull's-eye maculopathy
Bardet-Biedl and other syndromic retinal dystrophies
additionalInvestigations: Full-field electroretinography to confirm cone responses reduced disproportionately to rod responses
Multifocal electroretinography to map central cone dysfunction
Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the macula for outer retinal and ellipsoid zone loss
Fundus autofluorescence to detect bull's-eye or ring abnormalities
Colour vision and formal perimetry to characterise functional deficit
Molecular genetic testing with a retinal dystrophy gene panel
redFlags: Rapid central acuity loss in a young patient prompting urgent genetic and electrophysiological assessment
Features suggesting a syndromic association requiring systemic evaluation
Development of night blindness and peripheral field constriction signalling rod recruitment and disease progression
Family members with undiagnosed visual loss who may benefit from screening and counselling
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally worse than for many rod-cone dystrophies because central vision is lost early and progressively; most patients become significantly visually impaired, though the rate varies with the underlying gene.
pitfalls: Labelling the condition as retinitis pigmentosa and missing the cone-first electrophysiological pattern
Attributing an early bull's-eye maculopathy to drug toxicity without a genetic and drug history
Reassuring a patient that the disorder is stationary when it is inherently progressive
Overlooking a syndromic diagnosis by failing to take a systemic history
management: Provide low-vision rehabilitation with magnification and adaptive technology, as there is no established disease-modifying treatment
Manage photophobia with tinted lenses and advise ultraviolet protection
Offer molecular genetic testing with a retinal dystrophy gene panel and genetic counselling, and consider gene-specific therapeutic trials
Monitor progression with electroretinography, optical coherence tomography and perimetry as rod involvement and peripheral field loss supervene
Correct refractive error and optimise remaining vision
Arrange certification of visual impairment and educational, occupational and social support
Screen and counsel relatives according to the autosomal dominant, recessive or X-linked inheritance identified
